TXDR for outgoing command and picture bytes.

One address byte plus 128 pixels.

Clear every dirty bit when any one page succeeds.

Only successfully transferred pages may be marked clean.

topicTitle: The Trap — Clear, Then Redraw Everything

Drawing an identical final image can never create bus work.
Intermediate erase/redraw writes mark pages dirty.

Erasing changes lit bytes to zero and redrawing changes them back. Dirty tracking records actual intermediate changes even when the final picture is identical.

topicTitle: The Game Loop — Update at a Fixed Rate, Render When Time Allows

Drawing twice is necessary to make two elapsed steps count.
Catch up fixed simulation steps, then draw the final state.

State updates advance the simulation; intermediate pictures are optional.
Simulation updates follow the fixed deadline grid, while drawing need happen only for the final state. Catching up two updates preserves speed without two expensive flushes.

topicTitle: Why a Fixed Step — and the Spiral of Death

Every missed deadline can be recovered with unlimited catch-up.
Update cost exceeds the period, so backlog grows.

If update work exceeds the period, backlog grows as catch-up runs.
If each update consumes more time than its period, catching up creates further missed deadlines. The four-update cap drops unrecoverable elapsed time and permits rendering.

topicTitle: A Microsecond Stopwatch, Free, From SysTick

Only when the OLED has stopped acknowledging.
Give the OLED the highest priority because transfer is slow.

Independent fast deadlines motivate scheduling separation even when the display works.
Control needs urgency; bounded display work belongs at lower priority.

Read input only when a page is transmitted.
A one-call pressed edge may vanish between pictures.

Simulation updates can outnumber pictures; picture-based reads can skip edges.
pressed exists for only one pad_read call. Reading per rendered frame can skip edges when several updates are due.

const sprites are copied into SRAM on ARM by default.

The linker can place const in flash .rodata and ordinary ARM loads read it.

Fractional accumulation fixes simulation motion even before display transfer.

Always reverse both velocity components on every collision.
Use only the new position to identify the crossed face.

Entry direction determines the bounce axis; reversing both changes the trajectory incorrectly.
The old position distinguishes prior overlap from side entry.

question: Why can deterministic randomness improve game verification?

Known seed and input reproduce the same game results.
Unpredictable new seeds are necessary for exact regression hashes.
explanations: Reproducibility supports verification but does not by itself prove fairness.
A known seed and input script reproduce score, timing and framebuffer hash. This enables exact regression comparison without requiring unpredictable randomness.
A known seed and inputs are what make exact reproduction possible.

topicTitle: Sound — a Sequencer on a Timer
question: Why can a tone overrun its requested duration during a full flush?

OLED transfer stops the hardware tone immediately.
The requested duration is enforced independently by sound_poll during blocking I2C.

The timer keeps the previous tone active while software polling is blocked.
sound_poll cannot advance until the loop resumes.

Always; the tail cell is never occupied for collision purposes.
Only when it vacates during the same nongrowing move.
explanations: It is legal when that tail vacates during the same nongrowing move.
When growing, the tail stays and entering it is a collision.
Only when the tail vacates in the same move and the snake is not growing. Collision checks must precede destructive body mutation.

question: How does a bit-packed brick map make destruction cheap?
options: A linked-list traversal locates every brick object.
Mask one column bit; zero rows detect completion.
Clear the brick by OR-ing its bit into the row.
explanations: A bit mask directly identifies a column; no object traversal is required.
A column is one bit, so an AND mask removes it and all-zero row words detect wave completion. No per-brick object search is required.
OR sets a bit; an AND with the inverse mask removes it.

question: Why did flapping below the gap middle perform poorly?

Gap middle is always safest regardless of vertical dynamics.
An eleven-pixel climb can hit the gap’s upper pipe.
explanations: A flap climbs about eleven pixels and can overshoot into the upper pipe.
Input timing must account for predicted climb, which favored near-bottom triggers.
A flap climbs about eleven pixels. Triggering near the gap middle can hit its upper pipe; near-bottom timing leaves space for the climb.

question: Why delay button acceptance on the game-over screen?

It makes the checksum computation take 0.75 seconds.
The losing press must not dismiss its own result.

The input gate prevents the losing press from immediately dismissing the result.
The press causing the loss must not also dismiss its result. The 0.75-second gate gives a separate deliberate next action.

topicTitle: `$SCORE` — a Class Leaderboard With a Checksum

It occupies flash only because initialization is constant.

The program uses the mutable copy in RAM after startup.

Handler mode uses MSP even when the interrupted task used PSP.

question: Does unused stack pattern prove a task can never overflow?
options: Yes; untouched words prove every future path fits.
Yes; the pattern physically prevents writes beyond the stack.
No; it proves observed use, requiring margin.
explanations: They show observed use only; rare/deeper paths can exceed it.
A pattern is measurement/detection evidence, not a memory guard.
It measures the deepest use observed so far. Rare call paths and interrupt interactions still need stress and margin; a canary/high-water mark is evidence, not a universal proof.

options: read always returns exactly one UART byte.
Byte-stream reads may split or combine application frames.
read always waits until one full application frame arrives.
explanations: Buffering can return many bytes; the API does not define application boundaries.

A byte-stream read may split or combine frames; software must accumulate and parse boundaries.

question: What must a ring buffer distinguish?
options: Read/write positions, empty/full convention and overflow policy.
Only total array length; positions can be inferred from bytes.
head equal to tail can mean full and empty with no extra convention.
explanations: Read and write positions, empty versus full state, and what happens on overflow. Producer and consumer must publish positions safely; silent overwriting can corrupt messages.
The ring must track read/write positions and distinguish empty/full.
An explicit reserved-slot/count/state convention is needed to distinguish those cases.

question: What should a parser do with an excessive length or bad checksum?

Reject safely, bound waits and resynchronize.
Accept its valid prefix and ignore the checksum.
explanations: Waits and storage must be bounded; invalid frames need a resynchronization policy.

Partial plausibility does not establish length or integrity; reject and resynchronize.

question: What does open-drain mean for SDA and SCL?
options: Both lines actively drive high when no participant drives low.
Each participant needs a separate dedicated SDA wire.
Drive low or release; pull-ups establish high.
explanations: Open-drain participants release; pull-ups produce high.
Open-drain SDA/SCL support shared wires without opposing high/low drives.

question: Why use a repeated START for a register read?
options: It releases bus ownership so another controller can intervene.
It is an acknowledgment from the sensor.
Switch index-write to read without releasing bus ownership.
explanations: Repeated START preserves ownership while switching from index write to read.
START is a controller-generated transaction boundary, not an ACK.
It changes from writing the register index to reading from the same addressed device without relinquishing the bus, following the device’s transaction requirements.

question: When does a MAX7219 command take effect?
options: Immediately when the first MOSI bit is visible.
After the whole word shifts in and the latch rises.
As soon as TXE says the MCU buffer is empty.

A complete register/data word is shifted in using its specified clock order, then the rising chip-select/latch edge commits it. Seeing MOSI bits alone does not prove the device latched them.
Buffer room is not complete wire transfer or a rising latch edge.

question: Why can fixed-point multiplication overflow when the final answer would fit?
options: A fitting final result guarantees every intermediate fits.
The unscaled product needs a wider intermediate before rescaling.
Rescale after a narrow multiplication; shifting repairs overflow.
explanations: The unscaled product has more fractional bits and can require a wider range.
The unscaled intermediate product needs more bits than either operand. Widen before multiplication, then rescale and range-check.
Overflow has already discarded bits; widen before multiplying.

question: Does DMA make a buffer safe to read at any time?
options: Yes; DMA updates memory atomically as an entire buffer.
Yes; volatile alone establishes complete buffer ownership.
No; define completed-buffer ownership and overrun handling.
explanations: Individual transfers do not make a coherent whole-buffer snapshot.
Volatile does not stop concurrent DMA writes or define completion/overrun rules.
No. DMA and CPU are concurrent memory users. Establish which completed region belongs to the consumer, publish completion safely, and detect overrun before accepting a snapshot.

options: A request register readback proves RAM changed.
A zero-filled buffer always proves a zero-valued transfer.
Bounded completion plus observed buffer changes.
explanations: Configuration is intention; observe bounded completion and actual destination changes.
Zero may be unchanged memory; recognizable sentinels distinguish actual writes.

question: What does the saved PC help you find?
options: It identifies only the reporter's current instruction.
It always directly provides the failed data address.
Locate interrupted execution in the matching ELF.
explanations: The saved pc belongs to the interrupted/faulting context, unlike live handler pc.
pc locates execution; operand registers/instruction decoding may identify the data address.

question: Why read reset flags before clearing them?
options: Clear first so reading returns the newest historical cause.
Flags must never be cleared after recording.
Record the cause evidence before clearing it.
explanations: Clearing destroys sticky evidence; record documented flags first.
After recording, documented clearing permits later boots to distinguish new causes.
Clearing destroys the evidence distinguishing watchdog, software, power and other reset causes. Record the documented flags first, then clear them using the specified operation.

question: Why can “check work, then sleep” race?
options: An event can arrive between checking work and entering sleep.
A pending interrupt can never wake sleeping code.
The work check automatically disables every future interrupt.
explanations: An event can arrive between the work check and the sleep instruction. The sleep/wake protocol must make that transition safe and account for pending events.
The protocol must safely account for pending events and the transition race.
An event can arrive after the check and before sleep.

question: Why can moving a sprite leave a trail?
options: I2C checksums recreate the old background.
The old pixels were not erased or redrawn; dirty both regions.
Moving automatically erases pixels in the previous framebuffer location.
explanations: Checksums do not redraw the background; rendering must handle erasure.
The old pixels remain unless cleared or the old region is redrawn. Mark both old and new regions dirty, then transmit the changed bytes.
Old bytes persist unless cleared/redrawn; dirty both affected regions.

question: Why snapshot input events rather than just repeatedly read a held button?
options: A held level is identical to one press event.
Preserve transitions/counts instead of repeating held levels.
Repeated level reads always preserve every short edge.
explanations: A held button remains active across updates; a press is a transition/count.
Events represent transitions or counted actions. A held level can trigger an action every update, while an unpreserved short edge can disappear between updates.
A short transition can vanish between reads unless events are captured/preserved.

question: What belongs in a host test of game logic?
options: Measure target electrical current through host drawing hooks.
Treat successful host rendering as proof of target bus deadlines.
Repeatable rules, collision, boundary and state-transition checks.
explanations: Host game tests check deterministic logic, not physical electrical behavior.
Target timing, electrical behavior and CPU budgets still need target evidence.
Deterministic rules, collisions, boundaries and state transitions with repeatable inputs. Host success does not establish target bus timing, electrical behavior or measured CPU budgets.

question: How should trap and unaligned-load results be compared across silicon and an emulator?

Use one ELF from any build to decode both environments.
Assume both environments fault and omit the observed result.
explanations:

Record whether each faults, preserve the matching ELF and use stacked pc/lr to locate it.

Expected silicon behavior is a fault for both. emulator disagreement must be labeled.
Source addresses depend on the build; fault locations require the matching ELF.
An emulator may accept an unaligned load, so an expected silicon result cannot replace observation.

question: Why might removing the whole-line print mutex look harmless in an emulator?
options: A hardware UART automatically locks complete printf lines.
An emulator makes newlib formatting intrinsically reentrant.
Instant transmit may hide the concurrency race window.
explanations: The hardware transmits bytes; software must serialize complete messages and formatter calls.

Look for interleaved lines/checksum errors and explain why instantaneous emulator transmission may hide the race.

topicTitle: 3.3 V Is a Guess — Measure It

Use a zero calibration word as a valid zero-volt reference.
Validate factory/current VREF readings, then calculate VDDA.

question: What makes a predicted float-versus-integer multiply ratio a useful comparison?

Publish the predicted ratio as measured before running anything.
Compare different inputs chosen to make each format fastest.

A prediction does not establish runtime cost; actual execution and the stated timing model supply evidence.
Different inputs or work invalidate the comparison; the format must be the changed variable.

question: Why compare wrapping and saturating Q15 helpers before using their output as motor demand?
options: Wrap can reverse sign where saturation clamps the demand.
Wrap and saturation produce the same result at range boundaries.
Saturation recovers the exact out-of-range mathematical result.
explanations:
For 0.75+0.5, deliberate narrowing wrap gives -0.75 while saturation gives approximately +0.99997. The -1*-1 result is +1 and also needs positive saturation. Explain these boundary effects before sending results to an actuator.

Source workflow: contrast the deliberately wrapping Q15 addition with the saturating helper for 0.75+0.5 and -1×-1.

Explain the resulting sign reversal before using either result as an actuator demand.
They differ precisely when the exact value exceeds the representable range.

topicTitle: Measuring Cycles — SysTick as a Stopwatch
question: When target raw/net cycle counts disagree with the instruction model, what should be examined?
options: Multiplier, memory wait states and timer/overhead assumptions.
Treat modeled counts as guaranteed physical timing.
Change only the source line count until the numbers agree.
explanations:
Run the target arena and record both raw and net cycles. Compare with the instruction model under explicit multiplier, memory wait-state and timer assumptions; differences can arise from those conditions rather than arithmetic correctness.

Source workflow: run the target arena, record raw and net cycles and compare with the instruction model.

State multiplier, memory wait-state and timer assumptions when interpreting disagreements.
The model assumes a multiplier and memory behavior; physical flash waits and timer operation must be measured.
Source length does not determine instruction timing or timer overhead.

topicTitle: The ADC Side — Scan, Continuous, DMA
question: Before comparing polled ADC reads with DMA-buffer loads, what must be confirmed?
options: The DMA enable bit alone proves all three samples arrived.
Actual buffer writes and ascending IN0/IN1/IN4 order.
Compare loads from an unchanged zero buffer to real ADC reads.
explanations: Configuration does not prove transfers occurred; unchanged sentinel slots expose a missing data path.

On supported hardware, time three polled channel reads and three RAM loads from an active DMA scan. Verify all sentinel slots changed and that buffer slots correspond to IN0, IN1 and IN4 before comparing CPU cost.

Source workflow: time three polled (CPU repeatedly checks hardware status) channel reads and three RAM loads from a running DMA scan on supported hardware.

Confirm all recognizable initial marker (sentinel) slots change and buffer order is IN0/IN1/IN4 before comparing CPU cost.
Zero can be legal or unchanged RAM, so this could compare unrelated work without proving acquisition.

topicTitle: Memory to Memory — and a Surprise in `memcpy`
question: How should a 1 KB DMA copy be compared with linked memcpy on a Nucleo?
options: Infer Wokwi DMA performance from its configured transfer count.
Check every destination word and separate CPU availability from elapsed time.
Compare only return times and ignore destination contents.
explanations: Transfer count is setup intent; an unsupported model may never move data.

Use the actual linked memcpy and a word-width DMA copy, verify every destination word, then report elapsed transfer time separately from how much CPU can work meanwhile. Unsupported Wokwi should report failure/fallback instead of invented DMA timing.

Source workflow: on a Nucleo, race the 1 KB word DMA copy against the linked memcpy, check every destination word and report CPU availability separately from elapsed transfer time.

In unsupported Wokwi, report fallback/failure rather than inventing DMA timing.
A fast operation that failed to copy the data is not a valid speed result.

question: What establishes the result of an unaligned-access experiment in a particular environment?
options: Call a continued execution result proof that the access is portable.
Copy the ARMv6-M expected verdict without running the experiment.
Record fault or continued execution, then decode saved evidence.
explanations: An emulator accepting the access does not remove silicon alignment constraints.
Architecture expectations and model observations are distinct evidence.

Run the deliberate access and record whether the environment faults or explicitly reports continued execution. Decode preserved instruction and effective address. Do not assume simulator behavior matches ARMv6-M silicon.

Decode the preserved instruction and address. Do not assume simulator behavior matches ARMv6-M silicon.

topicTitle: Faults 2 and 3 — Nothing There, or Read-Only
question: If an ordinary flash store returns instead of faulting, what evidence should be recorded?

Assume every unmapped read and flash store has an identical cause.
The readback and FLASH->SR status, with outcome left observational.
explanations: An ordinary store is not the required programming sequence; controller refusal can return with status evidence.
Unmapped access and flash programming refusal/permissions are different paths that require different evidence.

Distinguish the unmapped read from the normal flash store. If the store returns, record readback and FLASH->SR. If it faults, reconstruct its address and permission verdict from saved evidence. The notes do not predetermine this runtime outcome.

topicTitle: Faults 6 and 7 — and Two Things That Do Not Fault
question: Why record actual NULL-read and variable divide-zero results even when execution returns?
options: The divide helper result must be identical in every linked build.
Any operation that returns without HardFault is valid C behavior.
A silent return can still reveal an invalid software operation.
explanations: The helper implementation and policy can differ; inspect the actual build and observation.
The absence of a core exception does not make NULL dereference or divide-zero a valid program operation.

Compare observed results with address-zero vector aliasing and the linked __aeabi_idiv0 behavior. A mapped NULL read or a divide-zero helper returning a value can hide a bug rather than making the software valid.

Explain why a silent return still represents a bug.

topicTitle: The WWDG — a Window, and a Shorter Reach
question: Before choosing WWDG feed timing for a nontrivial window, what must be calculated?
options: Only maximum expiration time; early feeding is always safe.
Tick period and the allowed counter interval.
Only the application loop count, regardless of the watchdog clock.
explanations: A window watchdog also resets if fed before the counter reaches the allowed window.

Calculate watchdog tick period and the permitted counter interval before selecting a refresh schedule. A feed above the allowed window can reset too early; allowing the counter to expire can reset too late. Both sides of the feeding window matter.

Source workflow: configure a nontrivial WWDG feeding window and explain both an early feed and late expiration.

Calculate tick period and allowed counter interval before selecting feed timing.
Counter progression is determined by its hardware clock and prescaler, not just loop iterations.

topicTitle: Measured — Who Feeds, Against What Failure
question: Which experiment fairly compares hb, loop and isr watchdog feeding policies?
options: Test one ordinary hang and assume it represents all failure classes.
Inject hang, IRQ-disabled hang and starvation separately for each policy.
Keep ISR feeding enabled during every policy comparison.
explanations: IRQ-disabled hangs stop a soft tick; starvation can leave loops or ISRs active. These distinguish policy coverage.

Select wdmode hb, loop and isr, then trigger an ordinary hang, an interrupt-disabled hang and starvation separately. Compare resets under the soft dog and supported hardware watchdog against the policy matrix, holding the workload/failure conditions consistent.

Source workflow: select wdmode hb, loop and isr and trigger hang, interrupt-disabled hang and starve separately.

Compare which failures reset under the software watchdog (soft dog) and under a supported hardware dog with the policy matrix.
That changes the refresh owner and can conceal failure, defeating comparison of the selected policies.

topicTitle: How Tight Can the Timeout Be?
question: What does five minutes of healthy operation near a reduced watchdog timeout establish?
options: A timeout based only on the fastest loop iteration.
A tested workload budget with measured gap and margin, not a universal bound.
A proof that every possible future path fits the timeout.
explanations: The longest healthy feed gap determines the required budget, including blocking work and margin.

Use stats worst-gap reporting while lowering wdt and include the blocking report in five-minute healthy trials. Record the exercised workload and chosen margin. The result covers those tested paths; rare unvisited paths can still exceed it.

Source workflow: use stats worst-gap reporting while lowering wdt until healthy use can survive five minutes, including the blocking report.

Record tested workload and margin. The result is a measured budget for those paths.
Finite trials establish observed evidence, not exhaustive worst-case timing for all paths.

topicTitle: Measured on the Host — What Dirty Pages Save
question: How should DIRTY and FULL display modes be compared using PERF output?
options: Compare fps alone and treat it as the simulation update rate.
Assume DIRTY always changes one page regardless of the game.
Compare traffic, flush duration, picture rate and update rate under the same workload.
explanations: fps measures pictures, while ups measures simulation steps; slow rendering can leave update cadence intact.
Tall moving pipes can dirty almost all pages; savings depend on the changed image geometry.

Use stick press to switch DIRTY/FULL and capture PERF bytes/frame, flush_us, fps and ups. FLAP changes nearly every page, so dirty transfer savings are limited. Bus-model durations depend on assumed rates and differ from observed target timing.

Source workflow: use stick press to switch DIRTY/FULL, capture PERF and compare bytes/frame, flush_us, fps and ups.

Explain why FLAP still changes almost every page and why bus-model time differs from target measurements.

topicTitle: Sprites — and Why `const` Is Enough on ARM
question: How should an ASCII sprite column be encoded for this OLED format?
options: Bit 0 is at the top; 0x25 lights positions 0, 2 and 5.
Each ASCII row is a separate full-byte brightness value.
Bit 7 is at the top; 0x25 lights positions 2, 5 and 7.
explanations:
Convert each vertical ASCII artwork column into bits with bit 0 at the top and cross-check using host/sprite.py. In 0x25, bits 0,2,5 are set. Store the resulting immutable column bytes in a const table.

Source workflow: draw a small ASCII sprite, convert each vertical column to bits with bit 0 at top, and use host/sprite.py to cross-check.

Decode 0x25 as lit positions 0,2,5 before inserting it into the const table.
The monochrome sprite packs vertical pixel presence into bits, not per-row brightness bytes.
That reverses the top-to-bottom mapping; the format uses least-significant bit at the top.

topicTitle: `$SCORE` — a Class Leaderboard With a Checksum
question: Why can a fabricated score still pass the classroom SCORE leaderboard checksum?
options: The sender can recompute the unkeyed XOR for the invented body.
A corrupted digit always remains valid without changing the checksum.
A checksum is a secret held only by the real game.
explanations:
Collect one captured SCORE file per honest player and run the leaderboard. Altering a digit without updating XOR is rejected; recomputing XOR for an invented score makes it pass. This detects some copying mistakes but does not authenticate honesty.

Source workflow: collect one text file of SCORE lines per honest player and run the leaderboard.

Corrupt a digit and confirm rejection. Then explain why recomputing XOR would make an invented score pass.
The demonstrated digit alteration changes XOR and is rejected; fabrication passes only with an appropriate checksum.
XOR uses public message bytes and no secret, so anyone can calculate it.

question: What evidence should accompany a fourth game added through the existing hooks?
options: Only source file sizes; those equal final linked RAM and flash use.
New memory totals, deterministic host behavior and the 20 ms update budget.
Only a screenshot; timing and linked memory remain unchanged automatically.
explanations: Linked sections, shared helpers and runtime allocations determine memory budgets, not source text length.

Use the existing input/update/draw/sound/score hooks. Budget RAM and flash, keep twenty-millisecond updates, and compare the new link-map totals and deterministic host behavior. Functional output alone does not establish memory fit or timing.

Source workflow: add a fourth game through the existing input/update/draw/sound/score hooks.

Budget its RAM/flash, keep twenty-millisecond updates and compare new link-map totals plus deterministic host behavior.
New game code/state can change RAM, flash and update cost; they need fresh evidence.
